A.explanation: Loss in gravitational potential energy minus work done against friction gives about $1850\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy.

B.explanation: This is approximately the $mgh$ lost, $2450\text{ J}$, with no subtraction of the $600\text{ J}$ done against the $30\text{ N}$ friction.

hints: Notice the 20 m is measured along the 30-degree slope, so find the vertical drop using $\sin30^{\circ}$ and the 25 kg mass.
Connect the vertical drop to lost gravitational potential energy $mgh$ and the 30 N friction over 20 m to work done against friction.
Compare the lost $mgh$ with the $F \times d$ work loss to find the remaining kinetic energy, starting from rest.
walkthrough: Find the vertical height lost after 20 m along a 30-degree slope: $h = 20\sin30^{\circ} = 20 \times 0.5 = 10\text{ m}$.
Calculate the loss in gravitational potential energy: $\Delta E_p = mgh = 25 \times 9.81 \times 10 = 2452.5\text{ J}$.
Calculate the work done against the constant frictional force: $W = Fd = 30 \times 20 = 600\text{ J}$.
Use conservation of energy from rest: gain in kinetic energy equals potential energy lost minus energy transferred by friction.
Substitute: $E_k = 2452.5 - 600 = 1852.5\text{ J}$, about $1850\text{ J}$ with unit $\text{J}$ checked. This is option A.
